description: Story logged: "Signal from the future." This is the same discipline that later spotted no-shows as a churn predictor: pattern recognition trained on the future.
notes:
STORY / PATTERN / PLAY format for the Signal pattern library:

Story: Optimiser teams resist reflection because it feels like falling behind. Mark reframed reflection as "imagine forward and name the signal you'd see" — gave optimisers a forward-leaning tool that did reflection's work without using the word.

Pattern: Optimisers will not stop to look back, but they will look forward. Reframe reflection as future signal-hunting and you get the same outcome with no resistance.

Play: Don't ask the team to reflect. Ask them to imagine the future state and describe the leading indicator that would tell them they got there.

description: Story logged: "The phone number that wasn't." At Missguided, customers complained constantly about the lack of a phone number. The team tested one and discovered young teenage girls don't use the phone — they panic when it rings. The real signal underneath the complaint was "I want a fast answer," not "I want to talk to someone." Team built an automated parcel tracker, which solved the actual job.
notes:
STORY / PATTERN / PLAY format for the Signal pattern library:

Story: Customers asked for a phone number. Team listened, tested it, watched what actually happened (panic), and built something completely different (automated parcel tracker) that solved the underlying need (fast resolution).

Pattern: The literal complaint is rarely the brief. Customers describe their need in the language of solutions they already know. The signal is in the job underneath, not the request on top.

Play: Take the literal request seriously enough to test it. Watch what people do, not what they said they'd do. Build for the job, not the request.

Strong candidate for early chapter or even introduction — accessible, specific, slightly funny, demonstrates the method with no framework needed first. Pairs naturally with the no-shows-as-churn-predictor story (also still to be formally logged) — both are "read the signal, not the surface" stories.

Reminder for next session: third story still to log — no-shows in client meetings as the leading indicator of churn, before the renewal call ever happens.

description: Story logged: "Give the analytics to finance." At Missguided, finance constantly picked apart eCommerce numbers in trading meetings. Mark noticed eCommerce was the only department with its own analyst — that asymmetry was the actual diagnosis, not the data dispute on the surface. He gave the problem to the loudest complainer, supported them with tech, and within months finance owned web reporting at 98% accuracy. The argument disappeared because the structure changed.
notes:
STORY / PATTERN / PLAY format for the Signal pattern library:

Story: Two functions kept fighting about the numbers. The fix wasn't better numbers or a better defence of the existing setup. It was handing ownership of the analytics to the team doing the picking-apart, and watching the dispute evaporate.

Pattern A: The structural asymmetry is the diagnosis. When something is arranged differently from everything around it, that arrangement is itself the signal. Most operators argue outputs; the move is to ask why the structure exists at all.

Pattern B: The loudest complainer is the best operator-in-waiting. People who pick apart a process have the strongest internal model of what good looks like. Give them ownership.

Play: When two functions are arguing about the truth, the answer is not better data. It is joint ownership of the data. Move the work, kill the fight.

Connections: This is the same operator instinct as the phone-number-that-wasn't story (read the signal, not the surface) and the no-shows-as-churn-predictor (look where others aren't looking). The meta-pattern across all four stories logged so far: the diagnosis is almost never where everyone is looking.

Strong candidate for the chapter on data, signal vs noise, or whichever Part Two chapter handles "where to look." Could also work as a worked example for the eCommerce/board gap material — board can't trust the numbers because the numbers are owned by the team being measured.

description: Surfaced and articulated the "room-shift move" — Mark's tacit intervention skill — through a forensic interview on five specific moments (Network advisory codes, Network tech roadmap, Network MAM, User Conversion / Sports Direct discount box, Travel Counsellors triangle). Pattern emerged from the detail rather than being imposed. Ready to add to Signal pattern library as the first articulated entry on the intervention half of the method.
notes:
SIGNAL PATTERN: THE ROOM-SHIFT MOVE

STORY (the trigger moment)
Network advisory away day. Board mapping out future strategy — full roadmaps, ambitious tech investment, BD targets, customer profiling work. Mark sat through the debate noticing the language was all outcomes, no inputs. Resource heavy and undefined. He silently scanned for what was actually defensible and one thing shone out: "people want codes that work." Customer reviews said it. Nothing else on the table felt like a moat.

He didn't announce it. He asked probing questions about which parts of the strategy were defensible and which would be removed by market shifts. The room narrowed toward the answer on its own. Then he asked one small concrete question: "so what are we doing to ensure codes work." The CEO got it first, then started asking others questions. Momentum built around it. Used the same hook later for the tech roadmap ("which part of this addresses broken codes, what if we focused only on that") and for the metrics question ("what's our key measure" — answer: monthly active members).

Same shape recurred elsewhere. User Conversion HR debate about flexible working: borrowed the Apple Regent St "we catch the bad guys" line to expose that the company was stifling 35 people because it worried 1 or 2 might take it too far. Sports Direct discount code box: a UI element causing frustration for millions, serving £10k a week of edge cases. Travel Counsellors 1:1 with the CEO: he drew a triangle of TC, Reps, Customers with the TC-Reps line as strongest; Mark added a complementary TC-Customers line rather than challenge the existing one.

PATTERN (the structural shape Mark hunts for)
A cost / benefit asymmetry where the room is investing heavily in something that doesn't justify it, while under-investing in something that would. Variants: optimising for the minority case at the cost of the majority. Adding capability the room can't defend while ignoring the one capability that's actually a moat. Building infrastructure for an edge case that hurts the main flow.

Two background filters running constantly:
- Design out: what here isn't essential?
- Simple is clever: what here can't be said without jargon?
Anything that fails either filter gets silently flagged.

PLAY (how the move is executed)

Prep before the room
- Map who is in the room, what each person believes coming in, who the unlock person is (usually most senior, the one whose nod releases the rest).
- Carry a curated library of external frames — stories from outside the industry with structurally similar shapes. Sourced from podcasts, magazines, life. Not quotes. Shapes.

In the room, two routes

Route 1 — Engineered narrowing (used when the answer is in the room but unspoken)
1. Probing questions about defensibility, cost, and "what would happen if we did none of it?" Inverts the frame from "what shall we add" to "what would we lose if we removed it."
2. Let the room's own logic narrow toward your answer.
3. Ask one small, concrete-sounding, tactical-feeling question that lands as the obvious next step. The smallness is the point. By the time it's asked, the strategic work is already done.

Route 2 — Borrowed frame (used when the answer needs to come from outside)
1. Reach into the library for an external story with the same structural shape.
2. Drop it in. Don't argue. The story sits there and the shape becomes visible.
3. Frames must feel weighty, not jovial. Apple lands. Funny anecdotes dissolve tension and let the room off the hook.

Three design rules across both routes
1. Aim at the unlock person. If they catch it, the room follows. Don't try to convince twelve people.
2. Refuse the binary. When pushback comes, separate the problem rather than rebut on its terms. "Well that's a different problem isn't it." Two problems become visible where the room saw one.
3. Add to their model, don't replace it. Use their language, their frames, their triangles. Sit your answer alongside what they already believe — complementary line, not competing one.

When it fails
- Frames pitched too abstract or too jovial don't land. Register has to feel weighty.
- If the unlock person doesn't catch it first time, switch routes. Don't hammer. Disagree and commit.

Engine underneath
Mark enjoys being clever. The move is craft, not technique. He distils naturally — can't help it. He grazes outside his own industry deliberately because competitors look backward at each other; he looks sideways. The library curates itself because of the pleasure he takes in compression and elegance.

NEXT STEPS
- This is the first articulated pattern on the intervention half of Signal. The diagnostic half is mature; this opens up the second half.
- Test the pattern against more recalled moments to confirm it generalises (Abbott Lyon data restructure was the trigger — should be revisited in detail to confirm route used).
- Consider whether Route 1 and Route 2 are two patterns or one with two modes. Current draft treats them as one move with two routes; may split later.
- Frame this for Backstage / Soundcheck: Backstage could surface the structural shape; Soundcheck could supply the diagnosis. The room-shift move itself stays human.

The borrowed frame step depends on two separately-learned skills:

1. Library curation. Mark grazes outside his own industry deliberately — podcasts, magazines, life. Things stick when they distil a structural shape, not when they're memorable quotes. The library curates itself because of the pleasure he takes in compression and elegance. Competitors look backward at each other; he looks sideways.

notes:
Skill packaged as asymmetry-spotter.skill, ready for installation.

WHAT IT DOES
- Hunts for cost / benefit asymmetries using two background filters (design out, simple is clever)
- Five variants documented: minority-vs-majority, undefendable capability vs moat, edge-case infrastructure, outcomes-without-inputs, outside-in vs inside-out

OPEN QUESTIONS TO RESOLVE THROUGH TESTING
1. Are all five variants real, or did some get inferred without enough evidence (variants 4 and 5 specifically — outcomes-without-inputs and outside-in vs inside-out)
2. Should the skill produce the probing question, or stop at the diagnosis and let Mark craft the question himself
3. The "unlock person" suggestion at the end depends on meeting-prep having run first — may need removing if it produces bad outputs when context isn't there

- Build follow-on skills: shapes-library (curated external frames) and room-mapper (prep discipline) once asymmetry-spotter is solid

notes:
FOLLOW-ON SKILLS BACKLOG

Both spawned from the room-shift move pattern (act-7743c1bef5b6503b). Sequenced after asymmetry-spotter (act-c63fcad2ffd40e54) has been tested and iterated.

---

SKILL 2: shapes-library

Purpose: Curated structured library of external frames with the same structural shapes as common business problems. Externalises the borrowed frame step of the room-shift move so Mark can pull candidates rather than wait for one to surface by feel.

Structure (proposed): Each entry has source, line, structural shape, tags, when used, outcome, register notes. Searchable by structural shape so a problem description returns matching frames.

Seeded by: act-34661d4e1cbadd5e (Apple Regent St, five-a-side team, condom failure example, Obama adjacent note, sourcing channels).

Risk: Externalising the library may kill the natural retrieval. Mitigation: library is a backup, not the primary route. Mark still hears things and they still stick. The library catches the ones that don't.

Build trigger: Once asymmetry-spotter is tested and either solid or clearly needs more shape variants, build this next.

---

SKILL 3: room-mapper

Purpose: The prep discipline. Given attendees for an upcoming meeting, produce a map of what each person likely believes coming in, and a hypothesis on who the unlock person is. Pulls from Lounge MCP (connection notes, triggers, prior interactions), LinkedIn, prior meeting notes, anything in Granola.

This is the bit Mark said he does for every meeting — currently in his head and takes time. A skill that does the first pass would compress prep without removing the judgement.

Should reference: Obama empathy practice (act-34661d4e1cbadd5e) as part of the discipline.

Pairs with: meeting-prep (the brief), asymmetry-spotter (the diagnosis), and the room-shift move itself. room-mapper produces the "who is in the room and what do they believe" input that the move depends on.

Build trigger: After Lounge MCP is more populated. Currently the connection records and triggers may be too sparse to feed this well. Worth waiting until there's more data to draw on.

---

SEQUENCING LOGIC

1. asymmetry-spotter [BUILT, pending test] — broadest application, every client engagement
2. shapes-library — value compounds with use, start small and grow
3. room-mapper — most data-dependent, benefits from richer Lounge MCP data

None of these replace the move. The move stays human because step four — the small concrete question, asked at the right moment, in the unlock person's language — is judgement under conditions a model can't see. What these skills do is take the prep load off so Mark arrives in the room with more bandwidth for the moment itself.

notes:
META-METHOD CAPTURED

Skill packaged as tacit-skill-extraction.skill, ready for installation.

WHAT IT DOES
Runs a forensic interview to surface a tacit operator skill that someone has but cannot articulate. Works for self-articulation (Mark on Mark, for Signal) and for client articulation (Mark on a client, for Backstage).

CORE DISCIPLINE — FOUR RULES
1. Refuse abstraction. Drift to principles → push back to a specific moment.
2. Refuse pattern-matching by the subject. They will compare moments too early. Stop them and stay inside one.
3. Refuse to lead. Don't suggest the answer. Don't name the pattern. The articulation must come out of their detail.
4. Refuse the throwaway. The offhand comments often contain the engine.

THE METHOD — SEVEN STEPS
1. Open with moments not questions (3-4 specific)
2. Forensic unpack on the first moment (slow, microscopic)
3. Repeat for two or three more (less depth, but still concrete; look for variance)
4. Look across the moments (hypothesise out loud, attribute every component back to a specific moment)
5. Test against a fresh moment (non-negotiable; otherwise you're over-fitted)
6. Draft the articulation (Story / Pattern / Play + engine + underlying disciplines + naming note)
7. Offer refinement (read it back, ask what's wrong)

CALIBRATED LENGTH
- Light (60-90 min): single skill, three moments
- Standard (90-120 min): default, three to four moments with full forensic depth
- Deep (multiple sessions): foundational skills, book chapters, senior hires

WHY THIS MATTERS STRATEGICALLY
This is the engine under Backstage. When Backstage runs operator articulation sessions for clients, this is the skill that powers it. It also means every future Signal pattern can be surfaced using the same method, so the book and the consultancy both compound on this.

Pairs with: asymmetry-spotter (once articulated, the skill's diagnostic logic can be applied), Studio Log (all sessions log at least one signal-story entry).

notes:
FORENSIC INTERVIEW SKILL

Skill packaged as forensic-interview.skill, ready for installation. 168 lines.

RELATIONSHIP TO TACIT-SKILL-EXTRACTION
Both skills share the same engine: four rules (refuse abstraction, refuse subject pattern-matching, refuse to lead, refuse the throwaway) and seven steps (open with moments, forensic unpack, repeat, compare, test, draft, refine).

The difference is what's being surfaced:
- tacit-skill-extraction: a specific operator skill someone has but cannot articulate. Output: Story / Pattern / Play. Highly specialised. For Backstage and Signal work.
- forensic-interview: anything else (idea, strategy, customer insight, decision, brief, hunch). Output: adapts to user's stated goal in step zero.

DESIGN DECISIONS
1. Generalised, not Network-specific. Reusable across any team Mark works with.
2. Step zero asks the user what they want to walk away with, so the variant is selected by them not by Mark or by Claude.
3. Five output variants documented: clearer idea, sharper strategy, surfaced insight, reframed brief, captured skill (latter points to tacit-skill-extraction).
4. Closing note on discipline included so users know what they're signing up for: "if the conversation feels comfortable, it's probably failing rule 3."

HOW TO INVOKE EACH SKILL

The skills fire automatically based on phrasing. Different phrases trigger different skills.

forensic-interview triggers on:
- "help me think this through"
- "I've got an idea but can't pin it down"
- "interview me on this"
- "run a forensic on this"
- "help me sharpen this brief / strategy / insight"
- "I keep going in circles on this"
- "I need to get clearer on..."
- "interrogate this with me"

tacit-skill-extraction triggers on:
- "help me work out what I'm actually doing when [X]"
- "I do this thing but can't explain it"
- "let's articulate this skill"
- "I want to capture this skill"
- "I'm running a Backstage session"
- "let's run a tacit skill extraction"

USE CASES
- Mark: forensic-interview when wrestling with a strategic idea or customer insight; tacit-skill-extraction when surfacing a Signal pattern or running a Backstage session
- Network team: forensic-interview for product decisions, customer insight surfacing, brief sharpening, strategic clarity
- Future Backstage clients: tacit-skill-extraction when articulating a senior operator's skill; forensic-interview when surfacing the strategic context around it
